Six of the fourteen summits of the Eight-Thousanders (Manaslu, Shishapangma, Cho Oyu, Lhotse, Mt. Everest and Makalu).

The [eight-thousanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eight-thousander "Eight-thousander") are the 14 [mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountain "Mountain") that rise more than 8,000 metres (26,247 ft) above [sea level](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_level "Sea level"). They are all in the [Himalayan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Himalayas "Himalayas") and [Karakoram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karakoram "Karakoram")[mountain ranges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountain_range "Mountain range"). This is a list of [mountaineers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountaineering "Mountaineering") who have died on these mountains.

### Mount Everest

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_deaths_on_eight-thousanders&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Mount Everest")]

Main article: [List of people who died climbing Mount Everest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_people_who_died_climbing_Mount_Everest "List of people who died climbing Mount Everest")

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d9/Mount_Everest_North_Face.jpg/250px-Mount_Everest_North_Face.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mount_Everest_North_Face.jpg)

North face of Mount Everest.

[Mount Everest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Everest "Mount Everest"), [Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth "Earth")'s highest mountain at 8,848.86 metres (29,031.7 ft) above [sea level](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_level "Sea level"), has been host to numerous tragedies. Deaths have occurred on the mountain every year since 1978, excluding 2020, when permits were not issued due to the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coronavirus_pandemic "Coronavirus pandemic"). The most notable deadly events on Everest were the [1922 British Mount Everest expedition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1922_British_Mount_Everest_expedition "1922 British Mount Everest expedition"), [1970 Mount Everest disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1970_Mount_Everest_disaster "1970 Mount Everest disaster"), [1974 French Mount Everest expedition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1974_French_Mount_Everest_expedition "1974 French Mount Everest expedition"), [1996 Mount Everest disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_Mount_Everest_disaster "1996 Mount Everest disaster"), [2014 Mount Everest ice avalanche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_Mount_Everest_ice_avalanche "2014 Mount Everest ice avalanche"), [2015 Mount Everest avalanches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Mount_Everest_avalanches "2015 Mount Everest avalanches") and [2023 Mount Everest season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_people_who_died_climbing_Mount_Everest#Background "List of people who died climbing Mount Everest"). As of December 2024, there had been 12,884 successful summits, and 340 people had died either before or after reaching the peak.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_deaths_on_eight-thousanders#cite_note-www.himalayandatabase.com-1) Since 2019 the Nepali government has initiated periodic "clean-up" campaigns on the mountain, including bodies of climbers.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_deaths_on_eight-thousanders#cite_note-2)

### K2

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_deaths_on_eight-thousanders&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: K2")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d0/K2_from_North.jpg/250px-K2_from_North.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:K2_from_North.jpg)

Northern vantage of K2.

[K2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K2 "K2") is the world's second-highest mountain at 8,611 meters (28,251 ft) above [sea level](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_level "Sea level"). It lies in the [Karakoram range](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karakoram "Karakoram"), partially in the [Gilgit-Baltistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilgit-Baltistan "Gilgit-Baltistan") region of [Pakistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistan "Pakistan")-administered [Kashmir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kashmir "Kashmir") and partially in the [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China")-administered [Trans-Karakoram Tract](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trans-Karakoram_Tract "Trans-Karakoram Tract") in the [Taxkorgan Tajik Autonomous County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxkorgan_Tajik_Autonomous_County "Taxkorgan Tajik Autonomous County") of [Xinjiang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xinjiang "Xinjiang"). While its summit is at a lower altitude than the summit of Mount Everest, it is considered a much harder mountain to climb due to its steep faces and extreme weather. The most deadly events on K2 were the [1986 K2 disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1986_K2_disaster "1986 K2 disaster"), [1995 K2 disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1995_K2_disaster "1995 K2 disaster"), and [2008 K2 disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_K2_disaster "2008 K2 disaster"). As of August 2023, an estimated 800 people had completed a summit, and 96 had died on the mountain.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_deaths_on_eight-thousanders#cite_note-3)

### Kangchenjunga

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_deaths_on_eight-thousanders&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Kangchenjunga")]

[![Image 83](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/33/Kangchenjunga.JPG/250px-Kangchenjunga.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kangchenjunga.JPG)

The summit of Kangchenjunga in the background.

[Kangchenjunga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kangchenjunga "Kangchenjunga") is the third-highest mountain in the world. Its summit sits at 8,586 meters (28,169 ft) in a section of the Himalayas called the Kangchenjunga Himal. Because of its remote location in Nepal and the difficulty of accessing it from India, the Kangchenjunga region is not much explored by trekkers. Despite modern improvements to climbing gear, the fatality rate of summit attempts on Kanchenjunga is high. While there had been 532 successful summits as of May 2022, 52 climbers had lost their lives on the mountain. 10 more climbers had died on Yalung Kang (Kangchenjunga West), one of several satellite peaks in the [massif](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massif "Massif"), which features routes to the summit of Kangchenjunga.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_deaths_on_eight-thousanders#cite_note-www.himalayandatabase.com-1)

### Lhotse

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_deaths_on_eight-thousanders&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Lhotse")]

[![Image 125](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/72/Lhotse-fromChukhungRi.jpg/250px-Lhotse-fromChukhungRi.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Lhotse-fromChukhungRi.jpg)

The south face of Lhotse, as seen from Chukhung Ri.

Standing at 8,516 meters (27,940 ft) above [sea level](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_level "Sea level"), [Lhotse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lhotse "Lhotse") is the fourth-highest mountain in the world. It is part of the Everest [massif](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massif "Massif"), and its standard climbing route follows the same path as Everest's [South Col](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Col "South Col") route up to the [Yellow Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Everest#Geology "Mount Everest") beyond Camp 3. After the Yellow Band, the routes diverge with climbers bound for Everest taking a left over the [Geneva Spur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geneva_Spur "Geneva Spur") up to the South Col, while Lhotse climbers take a right further up the Lhotse face. As of May 2022, there had been 1,089 successful summits and 22 deaths on Lhotse. A further 10 deaths had occurred on [Lhotse Shar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lhotse_Shar "Lhotse Shar"), a subsidiary mountain of Lhotse that offers a more difficult climb to Lhotse's peak than the standard route.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_deaths_on_eight-thousanders#cite_note-www.himalayandatabase.com-1)

### Makalu

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_deaths_on_eight-thousanders&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Makalu")]

[![Image 155](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/19/Makalu.jpg/250px-Makalu.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Makalu.jpg)

South-western vantage of the Makalu summit.

[Makalu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Makalu "Makalu") is the world's fifth-highest mountain at 8,481 meters (27,825 ft) above [sea level](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_level "Sea level"). It is located in the [Mahalangur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahalangur_Himal "Mahalangur Himal")[Himalayas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Himalayas "Himalayas") 19 kilometers (12 mi) southeast of [Mount Everest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Everest "Mount Everest") on the [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China")–[Nepal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nepal "Nepal") border. As of December 2024, there had been 800 successful summits of Makalu and 50 deaths on the mountain.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_deaths_on_eight-thousanders#cite_note-www.himalayandatabase.com-1)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

You can help by [editing the page](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:EditPage/List_of_deaths_on_eight-thousanders "Special:EditPage/List of deaths on eight-thousanders") to add missing items, with references to [reliable sources](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Reliable_sources "Wikipedia:Reliable sources").

[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/53/Flight_over_himalaya_annotated.jpg/250px-Flight_over_himalaya_annotated.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Flight_over_himalaya_annotated.jpg)

Six of the fourteen summits of the Eight-Thousanders (Manaslu, Shishapangma, Cho Oyu, Lhotse, Mt. Everest and Makalu).

The [eight-thousanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eight-thousander "Eight-thousander") are the 14 [mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountain "Mountain") that rise more than 8,000 metres (26,247 ft) above [sea level](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_level "Sea level"). They are all in the [Himalayan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Himalayas "Himalayas") and [Karakoram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karakoram "Karakoram")[mountain ranges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountain_range "Mountain range"). This is a list of [mountaineers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountaineering "Mountaineering") who have died on these mountains.

## By mountain

### Mount Everest

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_deaths_on_eight-thousanders&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Mount Everest")]

Main article: [List of people who died climbing Mount Everest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_people_who_died_climbing_Mount_Everest "List of people who died climbing Mount Everest")

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d9/Mount_Everest_North_Face.jpg/250px-Mount_Everest_North_Face.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mount_Everest_North_Face.jpg)

North face of Mount Everest.

[Mount Everest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Everest "Mount Everest"), [Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth "Earth")'s highest mountain at 8,848.86 metres (29,031.7 ft) above [sea level](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_level "Sea level"), has been host to numerous tragedies. Deaths have occurred on the mountain every year since 1978, excluding 2020, when permits were not issued due to the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coronavirus_pandemic "Coronavirus pandemic"). The most notable deadly events on Everest were the [1922 British Mount Everest expedition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1922_British_Mount_Everest_expedition "1922 British Mount Everest expedition"), [1970 Mount Everest disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1970_Mount_Everest_disaster "1970 Mount Everest disaster"), [1974 French Mount Everest expedition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1974_French_Mount_Everest_expedition "1974 French Mount Everest expedition"), [1996 Mount Everest disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_Mount_Everest_disaster "1996 Mount Everest disaster"), [2014 Mount Everest ice avalanche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_Mount_Everest_ice_avalanche "2014 Mount Everest ice avalanche"), [2015 Mount Everest avalanches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Mount_Everest_avalanches "2015 Mount Everest avalanches") and [2023 Mount Everest season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_people_who_died_climbing_Mount_Everest#Background "List of people who died climbing Mount Everest"). As of December 2024, there had been 12,884 successful summits, and 340 people had died either before or after reaching the peak.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_deaths_on_eight-thousanders#cite_note-www.himalayandatabase.com-1) Since 2019 the Nepali government has initiated periodic "clean-up" campaigns on the mountain, including bodies of climbers.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_deaths_on_eight-thousanders#cite_note-2)

### K2

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_deaths_on_eight-thousanders&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: K2")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d0/K2_from_North.jpg/250px-K2_from_North.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:K2_from_North.jpg)

Northern vantage of K2.

[K2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K2 "K2") is the world's second-highest mountain at 8,611 meters (28,251 ft) above [sea level](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_level "Sea level"). It lies in the [Karakoram range](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karakoram "Karakoram"), partially in the [Gilgit-Baltistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilgit-Baltistan "Gilgit-Baltistan") region of [Pakistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistan "Pakistan")-administered [Kashmir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kashmir "Kashmir") and partially in the [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China")-administered [Trans-Karakoram Tract](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trans-Karakoram_Tract "Trans-Karakoram Tract") in the [Taxkorgan Tajik Autonomous County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxkorgan_Tajik_Autonomous_County "Taxkorgan Tajik Autonomous County") of [Xinjiang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xinjiang "Xinjiang"). While its summit is at a lower altitude than the summit of Mount Everest, it is considered a much harder mountain to climb due to its steep faces and extreme weather. The most deadly events on K2 were the [1986 K2 disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1986_K2_disaster "1986 K2 disaster"), [1995 K2 disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1995_K2_disaster "1995 K2 disaster"), and [2008 K2 disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_K2_disaster "2008 K2 disaster"). As of August 2023, an estimated 800 people had completed a summit, and 96 had died on the mountain.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_deaths_on_eight-thousanders#cite_note-3)

### Kangchenjunga

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_deaths_on_eight-thousanders&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Kangchenjunga")]

[![Image 83](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/33/Kangchenjunga.JPG/250px-Kangchenjunga.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kangchenjunga.JPG)

The summit of Kangchenjunga in the background.

[Kangchenjunga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kangchenjunga "Kangchenjunga") is the third-highest mountain in the world. Its summit sits at 8,586 meters (28,169 ft) in a section of the Himalayas called the Kangchenjunga Himal. Because of its remote location in Nepal and the difficulty of accessing it from India, the Kangchenjunga region is not much explored by trekkers. Despite modern improvements to climbing gear, the fatality rate of summit attempts on Kanchenjunga is high. While there had been 532 successful summits as of May 2022, 52 climbers had lost their lives on the mountain. 10 more climbers had died on Yalung Kang (Kangchenjunga West), one of several satellite peaks in the [massif](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massif "Massif"), which features routes to the summit of Kangchenjunga.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_deaths_on_eight-thousanders#cite_note-www.himalayandatabase.com-1)

### Lhotse

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_deaths_on_eight-thousanders&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Lhotse")]

[![Image 125](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/72/Lhotse-fromChukhungRi.jpg/250px-Lhotse-fromChukhungRi.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Lhotse-fromChukhungRi.jpg)

The south face of Lhotse, as seen from Chukhung Ri.

Standing at 8,516 meters (27,940 ft) above [sea level](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_level "Sea level"), [Lhotse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lhotse "Lhotse") is the fourth-highest mountain in the world. It is part of the Everest [massif](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massif "Massif"), and its standard climbing route follows the same path as Everest's [South Col](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Col "South Col") route up to the [Yellow Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Everest#Geology "Mount Everest") beyond Camp 3. After the Yellow Band, the routes diverge with climbers bound for Everest taking a left over the [Geneva Spur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geneva_Spur "Geneva Spur") up to the South Col, while Lhotse climbers take a right further up the Lhotse face. As of May 2022, there had been 1,089 successful summits and 22 deaths on Lhotse. A further 10 deaths had occurred on [Lhotse Shar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lhotse_Shar "Lhotse Shar"), a subsidiary mountain of Lhotse that offers a more difficult climb to Lhotse's peak than the standard route.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_deaths_on_eight-thousanders#cite_note-www.himalayandatabase.com-1)

### Makalu

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_deaths_on_eight-thousanders&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Makalu")]

[![Image 155](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/19/Makalu.jpg/250px-Makalu.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Makalu.jpg)

South-western vantage of the Makalu summit.

[Makalu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Makalu "Makalu") is the world's fifth-highest mountain at 8,481 meters (27,825 ft) above [sea level](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_level "Sea level"). It is located in the [Mahalangur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahalangur_Himal "Mahalangur Himal")[Himalayas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Himalayas "Himalayas") 19 kilometers (12 mi) southeast of [Mount Everest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Everest "Mount Everest") on the [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China")–[Nepal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nepal "Nepal") border. As of December 2024, there had been 800 successful summits of Makalu and 50 deaths on the mountain.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_deaths_on_eight-thousanders#cite_note-www.himalayandatabase.com-1)

**Dhaulagiri**, located in [Nepal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nepal "Nepal"), is the [seventh highest mountain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_highest_mountains "List of highest mountains") in the world at 8,167 metres (26,795 ft) above sea level, and the highest mountain within the borders of a single country. Dhaulagiri I is also the highest point of the Gandaki river basin. It was first climbed on 13 May 1960 by a Swiss-Austrian-Nepali expedition. [Annapurna I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annapurna "Annapurna") (8,091 m (26,545 ft)) is 34 km (21 mi) east of Dhaulagiri. The [Kali Gandaki River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gandaki_River "Gandaki River") flows between the two in the [Kali Gandaki Gorge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kali_Gandaki_Gorge "Kali Gandaki Gorge"), the world's deepest.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaulagiri#cite_note-4) The town of [Pokhara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pokhara "Pokhara") is south of the Annapurnas, an important regional center and the gateway for climbers and [trekkers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trekking "Trekking") visiting both ranges as well as a tourist destination in its own right.

## Toponymy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dhaulagiri&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Toponymy")]

Dhaulagiri (धौलागिरी) is the [Nepali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nepali_language "Nepali language") name for the mountain which comes from [Sanskrit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanskrit "Sanskrit") where धवल (dhawala) means dazzling, white, beautiful[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaulagiri#cite_note-5) and गिरि (giri) means mountain.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaulagiri#cite_note-6)

## Geography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dhaulagiri&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Geography")]

Looking north from the plains of India, most 8,000-metre peaks are obscured by nearer mountains, but in clear weather, Dhaulagiri is conspicuous from northern [Bihar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bihar "Bihar")[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaulagiri#cite_note-indiamike-7) and as far south as [Gorakhpur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gorakhpur "Gorakhpur") in [Uttar Pradesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uttar_Pradesh "Uttar Pradesh"). In 1808, [survey computations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Trigonometrical_Survey "Great Trigonometrical Survey") showed it to be the [highest mountain yet surveyed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_past_presumed_highest_mountains "List of past presumed highest mountains").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaulagiri#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaulagiri#cite_note-FOOTNOTEColebrooke1818-9) This lasted until 1838 when [Kangchenjunga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kangchenjunga "Kangchenjunga") took its place, followed by [Mount Everest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Everest "Mount Everest") in 1858.

Dhaulagiri I stands to the east of the range which bears its name. Its sudden rise from lower terrain is almost unequaled—it rises 7,000 m (22,970 ft) from the Kali Gandaki River 30 km to the southeast, while the South and West faces rise precipitously over 4,000 m (13,120 ft). Such is its vertical relief that despite being closer to [Cho Oyu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cho_Oyu "Cho Oyu") and [Mount Everest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Everest "Mount Everest"), it is the only one of the Nepali eight-thousanders whose prominence parent is [K2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K2 "K2"), over 1,031 km (640 mi) away. The south face of [Gurja Himal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gurja_Himal "Gurja Himal") in the titular massif is also notably immense.

The rock layers found at the summit of Dhaulagiri, as well as Everest, are made up of limestone and dolomite formed at the bottom of the ocean. The summits of the other Himalayan [eight-thousanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eight-thousanders "Eight-thousanders") are made up of granite that was formed deep underground.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaulagiri#cite_note-10)

### Climbing history

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dhaulagiri&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Climbing history")]

[![Image 150](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c9/Sunrise_on_Dhaulagiri.jpg/250px-Sunrise_on_Dhaulagiri.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sunrise_on_Dhaulagiri.jpg)

The unclimbed South Face of Dhaulagiri, seen from [Poon Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poon_Hill "Poon Hill")

[![Image 151](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a0/Dhaulagiri_I.jpg/250px-Dhaulagiri_I.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dhaulagiri_I.jpg)

Dhaulagiri I in October 2002. The northeast ridge is the left skyline.

Dhaulagiri was the penultimate eight-thousander to be summitted, and the final in [Nepal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nepal "Nepal"). As its other routes are disproportionately dangerous, most ascents have followed the Northeast Ridge route of the first ascent, but climbs have been made from most directions. As of 2024, the two aspects which have repelled all attempts along their full length are the Northwest Ridge (though it has been climbed to the summit via the so-called "Pear" buttress) and the South Face. The latter is often regarded as one of the greatest remaining challenges in alpinism.

As of 2007, there had been 358 successful ascents and 58 fatalities, which is a summit to a fatality rate of 16.2%.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaulagiri#cite_note-11) Between 1950 and 2006, 2.88% of 2,016 expedition members and staff going above base camp on Dhaulagiri I died. On all 8,000 metre peaks in [Nepal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nepal "Nepal") the death rate was 1.63%, ranging from 0.65% on [Cho Oyu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cho_Oyu "Cho Oyu") to 4.04% on Annapurna I and 3.05% on [Manaslu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manaslu "Manaslu").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaulagiri#cite_note-Salisbury2007-12)

#### Partial timeline

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dhaulagiri&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Partial timeline")]

*   1950 – Dhaulagiri I reconnoitered by a [French expedition led by Maurice Herzog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1950_French_Annapurna_expedition "1950 French Annapurna expedition"). They do not see a feasible route and switch to Annapurna, where they make the first ascent of an [8000 m peak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eight-thousander "Eight-thousander").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaulagiri#cite_note-13)
*   1953–1958 – Five expeditions attempt the north face, or "Pear Buttress", route.
*   1959 – Austrian expedition led by [Fritz Moravec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fritz_Moravec "Fritz Moravec") makes the first attempt on the northeast ridge.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaulagiri#cite_note-hj_1959-14)
*   1960 – Swiss-Austrian expedition led by [Max Eiselin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Eiselin "Max Eiselin") makes the first successful ascent to the summit of Dhaulagiri.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaulagiri#cite_note-swi-15) Successful ascent by [Kurt Diemberger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kurt_Diemberger "Kurt Diemberger"), Peter Diener, Ernst Forrer, Albin Schelbert, Nyima Dorje Sherpa, Nawang Dorje Sherpa on 13 May.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaulagiri#cite_note-aj_1984-16) First Himalayan climb supported by the first prototype [fixed-wing aircraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pilatus_PC-6 "Pilatus PC-6"), which, after establishing the still standing record for highest fixed wing landing, eventually crashed in _Hidden Valley_ north of the mountain during takeoff and was abandoned.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaulagiri#cite_note-17)
*   1969 – American team led by Boyd Everett attempt southeast ridge; seven team members, including Everett, were killed in an [avalanche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avalanche "Avalanche").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaulagiri#cite_note-aaj_1970-18)
*   1970 – The second ascent, via the northeast ridge by a Japanese expedition led by Tokufu Ohta and Shoji Imanari. Tetsuji Kawada and Lhakpa Tenzing Sherpa reach the summit.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaulagiri#cite_note-aaj_1971-19)
*   1973 – American team led by James D. Morrissey makes the third ascent via the northeast ridge. Summit team: John Roskelley, Louis Reichardt, and Nawang Samden Sherpa.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaulagiri#cite_note-aaj_1974-20)
*   1975 – Japanese team led by Takashi Amemiya attempts southwest ridge (also known as the south pillar). Six are killed in an avalanche, including Norio Suzuki.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaulagiri#cite_note-aaj_2000-21)
*   1976 – Italian expedition makes the fourth ascent.
*   1977 – International team led by [Reinhold Messner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reinhold_Messner "Reinhold Messner") attempts the south face.
*   1978, spring: Amemiya returns with an expedition that puts five members on the summit via the southwest ridge—the first ascent not using the northeast ridge. One team member dies during the ascent.
*   1978, autumn – Seiko Tanaka of Japan leads successful climb of the very difficult southeast ridge. Four are killed during the ascent. French team attempts the southwest buttress (also called the "south buttress"), only reaches 7,200 m.
*   1980 – A four-man team consisting of Polish climbers [Voytek Kurtyka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voytek_Kurtyka "Voytek Kurtyka"), Ludwik Wiczyczynski, Frenchman René Ghilini, and Scotsman [Alex MacIntyre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_MacIntyre "Alex MacIntyre") climb the east face, topping out at 7,500 m on the northeast ridge. After a bivouac, they descend back to base camp in a storm. One week later they climb the mountain via the northeast ridge reaching the summit on 18 May.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaulagiri#cite_note-aaj_1981-22)
*   1981 – Yugoslav team reaches 7,950 m after putting up the first route on the true south face of the mountain, on the right side, connecting with the southeast ridge. They climb in alpine style but suffer four days of open bivouacs and six days without food before returning. Hironobu Kamuro of Japan reaches the summit alone, via the normal route.
*   1982, 5 May – Three members – Philip Cornelissen, Rudi Van Snick, and Ang Rita Sherpa – of a Belgian-Nepali team reach the summit via the north-east ridge. A day later, four more climbers – Ang Jangbu Sherpa, Marnix Lefever, Lut Vivijs, and Jan Vanhees – summit also. Vivijs becomes the first woman to reach the summit.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaulagiri#cite_note-23)
*   1982, 13 December – Two members (Akio Koizumi and Wangchu Shelpa) of the Japanese team led by Jun Arima of the Academic Alpine Club of [Hokkaido University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hokkaido_University "Hokkaido University") reach the summit. By the world calendar, winter begins 21 December, so this was not winter but a very-late-autumn-climb. However, the climb was done under a winter climbing permit, which the Nepali government issues for climbs beginning on or after 1 December.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaulagiri#cite_note-24)
*   1984 – Three members of the Czechoslovak expedition (Jan Simon, Karel Jakes, Jaromir Stejskal) climb the west face to the summit. Simon died during the descent.
*   1985 – Polish expedition led by Adam Bilczewski set out to conquer Dhaulagiri for the first time in winter. After seven weeks of dramatic struggle against hurricane-force winds and temperatures below −40c°, [Andrzej Czok](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrzej_Czok "Andrzej Czok") and [Jerzy Kukuczka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerzy_Kukuczka "Jerzy Kukuczka") achieve the first winter ascent on 21 January.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaulagiri#cite_note-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaulagiri#cite_note-26)
*   1986 – A mostly Polish expedition puts up a second south face route, on the left side of the face connecting with the southwest ridge route. They go above 7,500 m but do not reach the summit.
*   1988 – Soviet mountaineers Yuri Moiseev and Kazbek Valiev, in cooperation with Zoltan Demján of Czechoslovakia, succeed in climbing the southwest buttress. This 3,000-metre ascent, with difficult technical climbing at 6,800–7,300 m, was acknowledged as the year's best achievement at the UIAA Expedition Commission Conference.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]
*   1993 – Russian-British team puts up the direct north face route.
*   1995 — [Anatoli Boukreev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anatoli_Boukreev "Anatoli Boukreev"), speed ascent, record time 17 hours 15 mins, base camp to summit.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaulagiri#cite_note-27)
*   1998 – French climber [Chantal Mauduit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chantal_Mauduit "Chantal Mauduit") and Sherpa Ang Tshering die when an avalanche strikes their tent on the Northeast Ridge.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaulagiri#cite_note-aaj_1999-28) On 1 May the Greek climber Nikolaos Papandreou is killed falling in a gorge. On 2 October, the Greek Babis Tsoupras reaches the summit but does not return. The bodies of the Greek climbers were not found.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaulagiri#cite_note-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaulagiri#cite_note-30)
*   1999 – On 24 October, British climber [Ginette Harrison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ginette_Harrison "Ginette Harrison") dies in an avalanche on Dhaulagiri.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaulagiri#cite_note-Guardian1999-31) Days later, Slovenian [Tomaž Humar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toma%C5%BE_Humar "Tomaž Humar") climbs the south face solo but does not reach the summit. His ascent ended at 7,300 m due to a 300 m band of rotten rock. Humar traverses to the dangerous southeast ridge, re-enters the face briefly, and exits at 8000 m for a descent on the northeast ridge.
*   2024 – On 6 October, five Russians, Alexander Dusheiko, Oleg Kruglov, Vladimir Chistikov, Mikhail Nosenko and Dmitry Shpilevoy, went missing while climbing Dhaulagiri. Their bodies were found on 8 October.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaulagiri#cite_note-32)

**Dhaulagiri**, located in [Nepal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nepal "Nepal"), is the [seventh highest mountain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_highest_mountains "List of highest mountains") in the world at 8,167 metres (26,795 ft) above sea level, and the highest mountain within the borders of a single country. Dhaulagiri I is also the highest point of the Gandaki river basin. It was first climbed on 13 May 1960 by a Swiss-Austrian-Nepali expedition. [Annapurna I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annapurna "Annapurna") (8,091 m (26,545 ft)) is 34 km (21 mi) east of Dhaulagiri. The [Kali Gandaki River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gandaki_River "Gandaki River") flows between the two in the [Kali Gandaki Gorge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kali_Gandaki_Gorge "Kali Gandaki Gorge"), the world's deepest.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaulagiri#cite_note-4) The town of [Pokhara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pokhara "Pokhara") is south of the Annapurnas, an important regional center and the gateway for climbers and [trekkers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trekking "Trekking") visiting both ranges as well as a tourist destination in its own right.

## Toponymy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dhaulagiri&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Toponymy")]

Dhaulagiri (धौलागिरी) is the [Nepali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nepali_language "Nepali language") name for the mountain which comes from [Sanskrit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanskrit "Sanskrit") where धवल (dhawala) means dazzling, white, beautiful[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaulagiri#cite_note-5) and गिरि (giri) means mountain.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaulagiri#cite_note-6)

## Geography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dhaulagiri&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Geography")]

Looking north from the plains of India, most 8,000-metre peaks are obscured by nearer mountains, but in clear weather, Dhaulagiri is conspicuous from northern [Bihar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bihar "Bihar")[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaulagiri#cite_note-indiamike-7) and as far south as [Gorakhpur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gorakhpur "Gorakhpur") in [Uttar Pradesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uttar_Pradesh "Uttar Pradesh"). In 1808, [survey computations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Trigonometrical_Survey "Great Trigonometrical Survey") showed it to be the [highest mountain yet surveyed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_past_presumed_highest_mountains "List of past presumed highest mountains").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaulagiri#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaulagiri#cite_note-FOOTNOTEColebrooke1818-9) This lasted until 1838 when [Kangchenjunga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kangchenjunga "Kangchenjunga") took its place, followed by [Mount Everest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Everest "Mount Everest") in 1858.

Dhaulagiri I stands to the east of the range which bears its name. Its sudden rise from lower terrain is almost unequaled—it rises 7,000 m (22,970 ft) from the Kali Gandaki River 30 km to the southeast, while the South and West faces rise precipitously over 4,000 m (13,120 ft). Such is its vertical relief that despite being closer to [Cho Oyu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cho_Oyu "Cho Oyu") and [Mount Everest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Everest "Mount Everest"), it is the only one of the Nepali eight-thousanders whose prominence parent is [K2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K2 "K2"), over 1,031 km (640 mi) away. The south face of [Gurja Himal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gurja_Himal "Gurja Himal") in the titular massif is also notably immense.

The rock layers found at the summit of Dhaulagiri, as well as Everest, are made up of limestone and dolomite formed at the bottom of the ocean. The summits of the other Himalayan [eight-thousanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eight-thousanders "Eight-thousanders") are made up of granite that was formed deep underground.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaulagiri#cite_note-10)

### Climbing history

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dhaulagiri&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Climbing history")]

[![Image 150](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c9/Sunrise_on_Dhaulagiri.jpg/250px-Sunrise_on_Dhaulagiri.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sunrise_on_Dhaulagiri.jpg)

The unclimbed South Face of Dhaulagiri, seen from [Poon Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poon_Hill "Poon Hill")

[![Image 151](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a0/Dhaulagiri_I.jpg/250px-Dhaulagiri_I.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dhaulagiri_I.jpg)

Dhaulagiri I in October 2002. The northeast ridge is the left skyline.

Dhaulagiri was the penultimate eight-thousander to be summitted, and the final in [Nepal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nepal "Nepal"). As its other routes are disproportionately dangerous, most ascents have followed the Northeast Ridge route of the first ascent, but climbs have been made from most directions. As of 2024, the two aspects which have repelled all attempts along their full length are the Northwest Ridge (though it has been climbed to the summit via the so-called "Pear" buttress) and the South Face. The latter is often regarded as one of the greatest remaining challenges in alpinism.

As of 2007, there had been 358 successful ascents and 58 fatalities, which is a summit to a fatality rate of 16.2%.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaulagiri#cite_note-11) Between 1950 and 2006, 2.88% of 2,016 expedition members and staff going above base camp on Dhaulagiri I died. On all 8,000 metre peaks in [Nepal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nepal "Nepal") the death rate was 1.63%, ranging from 0.65% on [Cho Oyu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cho_Oyu "Cho Oyu") to 4.04% on Annapurna I and 3.05% on [Manaslu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manaslu "Manaslu").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaulagiri#cite_note-Salisbury2007-12)

#### Partial timeline

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dhaulagiri&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Partial timeline")]

*   1950 – Dhaulagiri I reconnoitered by a [French expedition led by Maurice Herzog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1950_French_Annapurna_expedition "1950 French Annapurna expedition"). They do not see a feasible route and switch to Annapurna, where they make the first ascent of an [8000 m peak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eight-thousander "Eight-thousander").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaulagiri#cite_note-13)
*   1953–1958 – Five expeditions attempt the north face, or "Pear Buttress", route.
*   1959 – Austrian expedition led by [Fritz Moravec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fritz_Moravec "Fritz Moravec") makes the first attempt on the northeast ridge.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaulagiri#cite_note-hj_1959-14)
*   1960 – Swiss-Austrian expedition led by [Max Eiselin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Eiselin "Max Eiselin") makes the first successful ascent to the summit of Dhaulagiri.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaulagiri#cite_note-swi-15) Successful ascent by [Kurt Diemberger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kurt_Diemberger "Kurt Diemberger"), Peter Diener, Ernst Forrer, Albin Schelbert, Nyima Dorje Sherpa, Nawang Dorje Sherpa on 13 May.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaulagiri#cite_note-aj_1984-16) First Himalayan climb supported by the first prototype [fixed-wing aircraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pilatus_PC-6 "Pilatus PC-6"), which, after establishing the still standing record for highest fixed wing landing, eventually crashed in _Hidden Valley_ north of the mountain during takeoff and was abandoned.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaulagiri#cite_note-17)
*   1969 – American team led by Boyd Everett attempt southeast ridge; seven team members, including Everett, were killed in an [avalanche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avalanche "Avalanche").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaulagiri#cite_note-aaj_1970-18)
*   1970 – The second ascent, via the northeast ridge by a Japanese expedition led by Tokufu Ohta and Shoji Imanari. Tetsuji Kawada and Lhakpa Tenzing Sherpa reach the summit.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaulagiri#cite_note-aaj_1971-19)
*   1973 – American team led by James D. Morrissey makes the third ascent via the northeast ridge. Summit team: John Roskelley, Louis Reichardt, and Nawang Samden Sherpa.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaulagiri#cite_note-aaj_1974-20)
*   1975 – Japanese team led by Takashi Amemiya attempts southwest ridge (also known as the south pillar). Six are killed in an avalanche, including Norio Suzuki.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaulagiri#cite_note-aaj_2000-21)
*   1976 – Italian expedition makes the fourth ascent.
*   1977 – International team led by [Reinhold Messner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reinhold_Messner "Reinhold Messner") attempts the south face.
*   1978, spring: Amemiya returns with an expedition that puts five members on the summit via the southwest ridge—the first ascent not using the northeast ridge. One team member dies during the ascent.
*   1978, autumn – Seiko Tanaka of Japan leads successful climb of the very difficult southeast ridge. Four are killed during the ascent. French team attempts the southwest buttress (also called the "south buttress"), only reaches 7,200 m.
*   1980 – A four-man team consisting of Polish climbers [Voytek Kurtyka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voytek_Kurtyka "Voytek Kurtyka"), Ludwik Wiczyczynski, Frenchman René Ghilini, and Scotsman [Alex MacIntyre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_MacIntyre "Alex MacIntyre") climb the east face, topping out at 7,500 m on the northeast ridge. After a bivouac, they descend back to base camp in a storm. One week later they climb the mountain via the northeast ridge reaching the summit on 18 May.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaulagiri#cite_note-aaj_1981-22)
*   1981 – Yugoslav team reaches 7,950 m after putting up the first route on the true south face of the mountain, on the right side, connecting with the southeast ridge. They climb in alpine style but suffer four days of open bivouacs and six days without food before returning. Hironobu Kamuro of Japan reaches the summit alone, via the normal route.
*   1982, 5 May – Three members – Philip Cornelissen, Rudi Van Snick, and Ang Rita Sherpa – of a Belgian-Nepali team reach the summit via the north-east ridge. A day later, four more climbers – Ang Jangbu Sherpa, Marnix Lefever, Lut Vivijs, and Jan Vanhees – summit also. Vivijs becomes the first woman to reach the summit.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaulagiri#cite_note-23)
*   1982, 13 December – Two members (Akio Koizumi and Wangchu Shelpa) of the Japanese team led by Jun Arima of the Academic Alpine Club of [Hokkaido University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hokkaido_University "Hokkaido University") reach the summit. By the world calendar, winter begins 21 December, so this was not winter but a very-late-autumn-climb. However, the climb was done under a winter climbing permit, which the Nepali government issues for climbs beginning on or after 1 December.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaulagiri#cite_note-24)
*   1984 – Three members of the Czechoslovak expedition (Jan Simon, Karel Jakes, Jaromir Stejskal) climb the west face to the summit. Simon died during the descent.
*   1985 – Polish expedition led by Adam Bilczewski set out to conquer Dhaulagiri for the first time in winter. After seven weeks of dramatic struggle against hurricane-force winds and temperatures below −40c°, [Andrzej Czok](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrzej_Czok "Andrzej Czok") and [Jerzy Kukuczka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerzy_Kukuczka "Jerzy Kukuczka") achieve the first winter ascent on 21 January.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaulagiri#cite_note-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaulagiri#cite_note-26)
*   1986 – A mostly Polish expedition puts up a second south face route, on the left side of the face connecting with the southwest ridge route. They go above 7,500 m but do not reach the summit.
*   1988 – Soviet mountaineers Yuri Moiseev and Kazbek Valiev, in cooperation with Zoltan Demján of Czechoslovakia, succeed in climbing the southwest buttress. This 3,000-metre ascent, with difficult technical climbing at 6,800–7,300 m, was acknowledged as the year's best achievement at the UIAA Expedition Commission Conference.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]
*   1993 – Russian-British team puts up the direct north face route.
*   1995 — [Anatoli Boukreev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anatoli_Boukreev "Anatoli Boukreev"), speed ascent, record time 17 hours 15 mins, base camp to summit.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaulagiri#cite_note-27)
*   1998 – French climber [Chantal Mauduit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chantal_Mauduit "Chantal Mauduit") and Sherpa Ang Tshering die when an avalanche strikes their tent on the Northeast Ridge.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaulagiri#cite_note-aaj_1999-28) On 1 May the Greek climber Nikolaos Papandreou is killed falling in a gorge. On 2 October, the Greek Babis Tsoupras reaches the summit but does not return. The bodies of the Greek climbers were not found.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaulagiri#cite_note-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaulagiri#cite_note-30)
*   1999 – On 24 October, British climber [Ginette Harrison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ginette_Harrison "Ginette Harrison") dies in an avalanche on Dhaulagiri.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaulagiri#cite_note-Guardian1999-31) Days later, Slovenian [Tomaž Humar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toma%C5%BE_Humar "Tomaž Humar") climbs the south face solo but does not reach the summit. His ascent ended at 7,300 m due to a 300 m band of rotten rock. Humar traverses to the dangerous southeast ridge, re-enters the face briefly, and exits at 8000 m for a descent on the northeast ridge.
*   2024 – On 6 October, five Russians, Alexander Dusheiko, Oleg Kruglov, Vladimir Chistikov, Mikhail Nosenko and Dmitry Shpilevoy, went missing while climbing Dhaulagiri. Their bodies were found on 8 October.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaulagiri#cite_note-32)

**Certina S.A.** is a Swiss watch brand, part of the [Swatch Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swatch_Group "Swatch Group"),[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Certina#cite_note-1) founded in [Grenchen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenchen "Grenchen") in 1888 by Adolf and Alfred Kurth. All Certina watches bear the "[Swiss Made](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swiss_Made "Swiss Made")" seal of origin.

Certina watches are not related to German industrial conglomerate [Certina Holding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Certina_Holding "Certina Holding").

## History of Certina S.A.

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Certina&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History of Certina S.A.")]

Certina S.A. was founded in 1888 when Adolf and Alfred Kurth opened in [Grenchen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenchen "Grenchen") their first movement and supplies factory for the watchmaking industry. At the start Certina's staff consisted of three employees working in a workshop that was connected to the family home. They did not begin producing complete watches and timepieces for a few years which they then did alongside their work producing movements for other companies. By 1938 the company had expanded and 250 employees celebrated the 50th anniversary of the company.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Certina continued to expand and by 1955 the company had 500 employees working between the factory and offices, producing 1,000 timepieces every day. Certina worked up a new business plan that expanded its operations.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

By 1972 the company employed 900 people and produced 600,000 watches per year.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

1983 Certina became a member of the SMH Group (Swatch). [[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Certina#cite_note-2)

## Affiliation to ASUAG

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Certina&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Affiliation to  ASUAG")]

In 1971, the owning family opted to join [General Watch Co](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Watch_Co "General Watch Co"), the newly created sub-holding of [ASUAG](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allgemeine_Gesellschaft_der_schweizerischen_Uhrenindustrie_AG "Allgemeine Gesellschaft der schweizerischen Uhrenindustrie AG"), in order to consolidate their efforts with others. The introduction of cheap and reliable [automatics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automatic_watch "Automatic watch") and [quartz watches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quartz_watch "Quartz watch") from Japan (under the ideas of their [strategic management](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strategic_management "Strategic management")) stopped Certina's expansion. The restructuring involved the abandonment of their own manufacture of [calibres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caliber_(horology) "Caliber (horology)"), and by the end of the 1970s, operations were moved to [Biel/Bienne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biel/Bienne "Biel/Bienne") and the entity [Edox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edox "Edox")&[Technos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Technos_(watches) "Technos (watches)"). Under the new management, the company managed to hold on to some of their properties, especially in the [Scandinavian countries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scandinavian_countries "Scandinavian countries"). Upon the merger of [SSIH](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SSIH "SSIH") and ASUAG companies, Certina S.A. became a member of a new managerial entity, together with [Mido](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mido_(watch) "Mido (watch)") and [Tissot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tissot "Tissot"), which became known as [Le Locle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le_Locle "Le Locle"), (the newly elected [Unesco World Heritage Site in Switzerland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_Sites_in_Europe#Switzerland_.2810.29 "List of World Heritage Sites in Europe")).[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

## Wristwatches, world’s first & lines of collection

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Certina&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Wristwatches, world’s first & lines of collection")]

*   The first wristwatches: were already produced by the company in 1938: predominately ladies watches, because men still preferred pocket watches.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]
*   Digital Watch: 1936 became the first company to produce a digital watch. It was driven by a spring movement. Rotating disks bearing inscribed numbers were used to display the time, instead of hands.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]
*   DS (Double Security) Line: In 1959 Hans and Edwin Kurth set themselves the objective of creating a new marketplace niche based on quality through engineering and technical design. Thus the company created the concept of suspending the watch movement inside a highly reinforced case, which was named DS after "Double Security". These were the first watches to increase shock protection and water resistance to 6 m (previous watches were set at 2.2 metres). The watch was taken up the Himalayas by a team who climbed the Dhaulagiri and the watch withstood all changes in pressure and altitude.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]
*   Biostar: In 1971 introduced the Biostar, the world's first watch that displayed human biorhythms.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]
*   "Scratchproof": produced the "unscratchable" DS-DiaMaster in [tungsten carbide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tungsten_carbide "Tungsten carbide").

Recent collection of Certina S.A. include [Titanium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titanium "Titanium"), [316L](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/316L "316L") high grade stainless steel, [sapphire glass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sapphire#Synthetic_sapphire "Sapphire"), its own DS feature (such as the current "DS Podium", "DS First" or "DS Action") and [ETA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ETA_SA "ETA SA") Swiss made movements are standard features. ## Marketing

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Certina&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Marketing")]

Certina S.A. has partnered with motoring companies including [Colin McRae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colin_McRae "Colin McRae"), [Sete Gibernau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sete_Gibernau "Sete Gibernau"), [Sauber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sauber "Sauber")[Formula One](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Formula_One "Formula One") team.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Certina S.A. was timekeeper of the [Motorcycling Grand Prix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Prix_motorcycle_racing "Grand Prix motorcycle racing") in the 1990s.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Certina S.A. sponsored the 2014 [World Rally Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Rally_Championship "World Rally Championship").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

## The Certina brand

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Certina&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: The Certina brand")]

In 1906 the Certina brand name was used for the first time, with Adolf and Alfred choosing to call their watches "Grana", the short form of "Granatus", the Latin name for [Grenchen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenchen "Grenchen").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In 1938 the company adopted the name "Certina", taken from the Latin "certus", meaning "assured", "certain", as their trademark for the export and marketing of their watches.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In 2014 Certina S.A. changed their red logo with a new logo. The new logo uses a turtle symbol, to symbolize protection against water and shocks. The change in logo and brand colours was because Certina S.A. wanted to move to a more expensive and higher quality segment, differentiating it from [Tissot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tissot "Tissot"), another brand in the [Swatch Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swatch_Group "Swatch Group") family. The impact of the changes in the brand has been the integration of better and more accurate movements like the PreciDrive in new releases.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

**Certina S.A.** is a Swiss watch brand, part of the [Swatch Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swatch_Group "Swatch Group"),[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Certina#cite_note-1) founded in [Grenchen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenchen "Grenchen") in 1888 by Adolf and Alfred Kurth. All Certina watches bear the "[Swiss Made](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swiss_Made "Swiss Made")" seal of origin.

Certina watches are not related to German industrial conglomerate [Certina Holding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Certina_Holding "Certina Holding").

## History of Certina S.A.

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Certina&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History of Certina S.A.")]

Certina S.A. was founded in 1888 when Adolf and Alfred Kurth opened in [Grenchen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenchen "Grenchen") their first movement and supplies factory for the watchmaking industry. At the start Certina's staff consisted of three employees working in a workshop that was connected to the family home. They did not begin producing complete watches and timepieces for a few years which they then did alongside their work producing movements for other companies. By 1938 the company had expanded and 250 employees celebrated the 50th anniversary of the company.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Certina continued to expand and by 1955 the company had 500 employees working between the factory and offices, producing 1,000 timepieces every day. Certina worked up a new business plan that expanded its operations.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

By 1972 the company employed 900 people and produced 600,000 watches per year.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

1983 Certina became a member of the SMH Group (Swatch). [[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Certina#cite_note-2)

## Affiliation to ASUAG

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Certina&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Affiliation to  ASUAG")]

In 1971, the owning family opted to join [General Watch Co](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Watch_Co "General Watch Co"), the newly created sub-holding of [ASUAG](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allgemeine_Gesellschaft_der_schweizerischen_Uhrenindustrie_AG "Allgemeine Gesellschaft der schweizerischen Uhrenindustrie AG"), in order to consolidate their efforts with others. The introduction of cheap and reliable [automatics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automatic_watch "Automatic watch") and [quartz watches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quartz_watch "Quartz watch") from Japan (under the ideas of their [strategic management](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strategic_management "Strategic management")) stopped Certina's expansion. The restructuring involved the abandonment of their own manufacture of [calibres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caliber_(horology) "Caliber (horology)"), and by the end of the 1970s, operations were moved to [Biel/Bienne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biel/Bienne "Biel/Bienne") and the entity [Edox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edox "Edox")&[Technos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Technos_(watches) "Technos (watches)"). Under the new management, the company managed to hold on to some of their properties, especially in the [Scandinavian countries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scandinavian_countries "Scandinavian countries"). Upon the merger of [SSIH](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SSIH "SSIH") and ASUAG companies, Certina S.A. became a member of a new managerial entity, together with [Mido](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mido_(watch) "Mido (watch)") and [Tissot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tissot "Tissot"), which became known as [Le Locle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le_Locle "Le Locle"), (the newly elected [Unesco World Heritage Site in Switzerland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_Sites_in_Europe#Switzerland_.2810.29 "List of World Heritage Sites in Europe")).[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

## Wristwatches, world’s first & lines of collection

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Certina&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Wristwatches, world’s first & lines of collection")]

*   The first wristwatches: were already produced by the company in 1938: predominately ladies watches, because men still preferred pocket watches.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]
*   Digital Watch: 1936 became the first company to produce a digital watch. It was driven by a spring movement. Rotating disks bearing inscribed numbers were used to display the time, instead of hands.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]
*   DS (Double Security) Line: In 1959 Hans and Edwin Kurth set themselves the objective of creating a new marketplace niche based on quality through engineering and technical design. Thus the company created the concept of suspending the watch movement inside a highly reinforced case, which was named DS after "Double Security". These were the first watches to increase shock protection and water resistance to 6 m (previous watches were set at 2.2 metres). The watch was taken up the Himalayas by a team who climbed the Dhaulagiri and the watch withstood all changes in pressure and altitude.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]
*   Biostar: In 1971 introduced the Biostar, the world's first watch that displayed human biorhythms.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]
*   "Scratchproof": produced the "unscratchable" DS-DiaMaster in [tungsten carbide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tungsten_carbide "Tungsten carbide").

## Advanced Systems and Materials

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Certina&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Advanced Systems and Materials")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/14/CertinaBasic.JPG/250px-CertinaBasic.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:CertinaBasic.JPG)

Certina Basic

Recent collection of Certina S.A. include [Titanium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titanium "Titanium"), [316L](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/316L "316L") high grade stainless steel, [sapphire glass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sapphire#Synthetic_sapphire "Sapphire"), its own DS feature (such as the current "DS Podium", "DS First" or "DS Action") and [ETA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ETA_SA "ETA SA") Swiss made movements are standard features. It currently offers collections, classified under the names "Automatic", "SPORT Classic", "SPORT Elegant" and "SPORT Xtreme", including some models claimed to perform up to 300 m underwater.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

## Marketing

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Certina&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Marketing")]

Certina S.A. has partnered with motoring companies including [Colin McRae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colin_McRae "Colin McRae"), [Sete Gibernau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sete_Gibernau "Sete Gibernau"), [Sauber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sauber "Sauber")[Formula One](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Formula_One "Formula One") team.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Certina S.A. was timekeeper of the [Motorcycling Grand Prix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Prix_motorcycle_racing "Grand Prix motorcycle racing") in the 1990s.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Certina S.A. sponsored the 2014 [World Rally Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Rally_Championship "World Rally Championship").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

## The Certina brand

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Certina&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: The Certina brand")]

In 1906 the Certina brand name was used for the first time, with Adolf and Alfred choosing to call their watches "Grana", the short form of "Granatus", the Latin name for [Grenchen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenchen "Grenchen").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In 1938 the company adopted the name "Certina", taken from the Latin "certus", meaning "assured", "certain", as their trademark for the export and marketing of their watches.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In 2014 Certina S.A. changed their red logo with a new logo. The new logo uses a turtle symbol, to symbolize protection against water and shocks. The change in logo and brand colours was because Certina S.A. wanted to move to a more expensive and higher quality segment, differentiating it from [Tissot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tissot "Tissot"), another brand in the [Swatch Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swatch_Group "Swatch Group") family. The impact of the changes in the brand has been the integration of better and more accurate movements like the PreciDrive in new releases.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

**Annapurna** ([/ˌ æ n ə ˈ p ʊər n ə ˌ-ˈ p ɜːr-/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English");[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annapurna_I#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annapurna_I#cite_note-7)[Nepali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nepali_language "Nepali language"): [अन्नपूर्ण](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%E0%A4%85%E0%A4%A8%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%A8%E0%A4%AA%E0%A5%82%E0%A4%B0%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%A3 "wikt:अन्नपूर्ण")) is a [mountain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountain "Mountain") situated in the [Annapurna mountain range](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annapurna_(mountain_range) "Annapurna (mountain range)") of [Gandaki Province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gandaki_Province "Gandaki Province"), north-central [Nepal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nepal "Nepal"). It is the [10th highest mountain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_highest_mountains_on_Earth "List of highest mountains on Earth") in the world at 8,091 metres (26,545 ft) above sea level and is well known for the difficulty and danger involved in its ascent.

[Maurice Herzog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurice_Herzog "Maurice Herzog") led a [French expedition to its summit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1950_French_Annapurna_expedition "1950 French Annapurna expedition") through the north face in 1950, making it the first [eight-thousander](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eight-thousander "Eight-thousander") to be successfully climbed.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annapurna_I#cite_note-8) The entire massif and surrounding area are protected within the 7,629-square-kilometre (2,946 mi 2)[Annapurna Conservation Area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annapurna_Conservation_Area "Annapurna Conservation Area"), the first and largest conservation area in Nepal. The Annapurna Conservation Area is home to several world-class [treks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Backpacking_(wilderness) "Backpacking (wilderness)"), including [Annapurna Sanctuary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annapurna_Sanctuary "Annapurna Sanctuary") and [Annapurna Circuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annapurna_Circuit "Annapurna Circuit").

For decades, Annapurna I held the highest fatality-to-summit rate of all principal eight-thousander summits; it has, however, seen great climbing successes in recent years, with a current fatality rate of approximately 13.42% (75 deaths from 559 ascents), according to [Guinness World Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guinness_World_Records "Guinness World Records").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annapurna_I#cite_note-gwr-annapurna-9) The mountain still poses grave threats to climbers through avalanche danger, unpredictable weather and the extremely steep and committing nature of its climbing routes, in particular its 3,000-metre (9,800 ft) south face, renowned as one of the most difficult climbs in the world.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annapurna_I#cite_note-10) It is also a dangerous peak for trekkers, as in the case of [a 2014 snowstorm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_Nepal_snowstorm_disaster "2014 Nepal snowstorm disaster") near it and Dhaulagiri which killed at least 43 people. As of February 2025, 559 people had reached the summit of Annapurna I, while 75 had died in the attempt.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annapurna_I#cite_note-gwr-annapurna-9)

## Etymology

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Annapurna&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Etymology")]

The mountain is named after [Annapurna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annapurna_(goddess) "Annapurna (goddess)"), the Hindu goddess of food and nourishment, who is said to reside there. The name Annapurna is derived from the [Sanskrit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanskrit "Sanskrit")-language words _purna_ ("filled") and _anna_ ("food"), and can be translated as "everlasting food".[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annapurna_I#cite_note-Loar2011-11) Many streams descending from the slopes of the Annapurna Massif provide water for the agricultural fields and pastures located at lower elevations.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annapurna_I#cite_note-Frankel2003-12)

## Geology

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Annapurna&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Geology")]

Annapurna Mountain consists of a few-kilometre-thick stack of early [Paleozoic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paleozoic "Paleozoic")[sedimentary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sedimentary "Sedimentary") and [metasedimentary rocks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metasedimentary_rock "Metasedimentary rock") of the [Tethyan Himalayan Sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pre-collisional_Himalaya "Pre-collisional Himalaya") that steeply [dips northward](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strike_and_dip "Strike and dip"). From top to bottom these sedimentary rocks consist of [Ordovician](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordovician "Ordovician")[limestone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limestone "Limestone"), [dolomite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dolomite_(rock) "Dolomite (rock)"), calc-[schist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schist "Schist"), [shale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shale "Shale"), and [sandstone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandstone "Sandstone") of the Nilgiri Formation; [Cambrian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambrian "Cambrian")[psammite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psammite "Psammite"), [marble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marble "Marble"), and sandstone of the Annapurna Yellow Formation; and Cambrian [pelitic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pelitic "Pelitic") and the highly deformed, semipelitic schists of the Sanctuary Formation. These northerly tilted (dipping) layers of sedimentary rocks are the northern [limb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anticline "Anticline") of the overturned Nilgiri [Anticline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anticline "Anticline"). The summit of Annapurna consists of the Nilgiri Formation.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annapurna_I#cite_note-GodinOthers1981a-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annapurna_I#cite_note-ParsonOthers2016a-14)

Tethyan Himalayan Sequence consists of a 11-kilometre (6.8 mi) thick pile of [Neoproterozoic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neoproterozoic "Neoproterozoic") to [Mesozoic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesozoic "Mesozoic") sedimentary rocks that accumulated within a prehistoric [continental shelf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continental_shelf "Continental shelf"). This continental shelf was located along the northern shore of the Indian subcontinent and submerged beneath southern margin of the prehistoric [Tethys Ocean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tethys_Ocean "Tethys Ocean") prior its collision with Asia. The collision of India and Asia during the [Himalayan orogeny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Himalayan_orogeny "Himalayan orogeny") incorporated this continental shelf into the Himalayan Mountains as a thin, [fault-bounded](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fault_(geology) "Fault (geology)") tectonic package of rocks that outcrops continuously for more than 2,000-kilometre (1,200 mi) along the length of the Himalayan Mountains.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annapurna_I#cite_note-GodinOthers1981a-13)

## Climbing history

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Annapurna&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Climbing history")]

### Climbing expeditions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Annapurna&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Climbing expeditions")]
